constitutive_assumptions: Plane sections of the cable are allowed to warp due to wire slip (PAGE 14).
Cable material is assumed to be homogeneous, isotropic, and linearly elastic (PAGE 14).
Strains are assumed to be small; shear deformation and Poisson's effects are neglected (PAGE 14).
Kinetic friction is neglected in the frictional bending model (PAGE 14).
Elongation of the cable caused by axial tension is neglected (PAGE 14).
Gravitational forces on the cable segment are neglected (PAGE 15).
Cross-sectional area and mass density are assumed constant along the uniform cable (PAGE 16).
Axial tension is approximated as constant during small vibrations (PAGE 16).
Flexural rigidity (EI) is assumed to be constant along the length of each individual cable element (PAGE 22).
The entire cable is idealized and modeled as a one-dimensional continuum with variable flexural rigidity (PAGE 13, 56).
control_variables: Cable geometric parameters: core wire diameter (2.12 mm), layer 2 wire diameter (2.0 mm, 6 wires, lay length 41 mm, lay angle -17.52 deg), layer 3 wire diameter (2.0 mm, 12 wires, lay length 90 mm, lay angle 15.82 deg), total 19 wires (PAGE 21).
Cable material parameters: elastic modulus (200,000 MPa), Poisson's ratio (0.29), static friction coefficient (0.74), kinetic friction coefficient (0.57) (PAGE 21).
Cable specimen length: 1.0 m for simply-supported case, 0.3 m for cantilever case (PAGE 35, 42, 49).
Finite element element length: 0.05 m (half of longest lay length) for simply-supported, 0.015 m for cantilever (PAGE 37, 43).
Time integration step size: 1/320 s for simply-supported cable, 1/100 s for cantilever cable (PAGE 37, 43).
Newmark numerical integration parameters: beta = 0.25, gamma = 0.5 (PAGE 27, 32, 37, 43).
Instron test parameters: test speed of 1 in/min, 500 N load cell (PAGE 61).
dependent_variables: Transverse vertical displacement w(x, t) along the cable length over time (PAGE 15, 22, 37, 44, 53).
Bending curvature kappa along the cable (PAGE 16, 18).
Variable flexural rigidity EI as a function of bending curvature (PAGE 16, 17, 18).
Static friction force between adjacent wire layers (PAGE 58, 63, 65).
Interlayer normal force and interlayer radial pressure (PAGE 63, 65).
Force-displacement hysteresis loops under cyclic loading (PAGE 52, 54).
Nodal velocities and accelerations during time-stepping simulation (PAGE 28).

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Energy dissipation and vibration amplitude reduction in multi-layered helical cables occur as a result of internal dry friction when bending deformations cause relative wire slippage between adjacent layers.

Flexural rigidity of a multi-layer helical cable exhibits nonlinear variation with bending curvature, remaining at a maximum constant value until critical curvatures are reached where interlayer shear forces overcome frictional resistance and wire slippage begins.

Under free vibration, the transverse displacement history exhibits an initial damped vibration regime where large curvatures induce wire slipping and frictional dissipation, followed by an undamped small-amplitude vibration regime once curvature drops below the slip threshold.

Interlayer static friction forces and normal pressures in helical cable layers can be experimentally measured using axial compression slip tests on dissected cable specimens in a materials testing machine.

A one-dimensional continuum dynamic model discretized with fifth-order Hermite interpolation elements and integrated via Newmark's method qualitatively predicts displacement histories and forced vibration hysteresis within 10% error of experimental data.

experimental_setup: Instron Model 4206 materials testing machine with a 500 N load cell running at a test speed of 1 in/min coupled to a data recorder to measure static friction forces between cable layers (PAGE 58, 60, 61, 62).

Two-hole test table holding dissected cable specimens: Specimen 1 (layers 2 and 3 cut off) to test layer 1-2 interface, and Specimen 2 (layer 3 cut off) to test layer 2-3 interface during axial compression (PAGE 58, 59, 60, 62).

Forced vibration experimental setup (from Sauter and Hagedorn 2002 cited for model validation) consisting of a 0.3 m cantilever cable clamped at one end and driven at the free end by a low-frequency cyclic transverse force of 15 N with a 6-second period to neglect inertia effects (PAGE 49, 50).
future_work: Extend the analytical bending model to include the effects of torsion, axial elongation, interlayer pressures, and geometric and material nonlinearities into an updated stiffness matrix (PAGE 57).
Perform more accurate experimental determinations of interlayer radial pressure, such as using pressure-indicating sensor films (PAGE 57).
Incorporate internal material damping as well as external damping effects to formulate damped cable vibration (PAGE 57).
Apply large motion and deformation theory to replace the current small deformation assumption for more realistic dynamic results (PAGE 57).
independent_variables: Time t and discrete time step Delta t (PAGE 26, 37, 43).
Axial coordinate x along the cable span (PAGE 15, 20, 35, 42).
Applied cyclic transverse forcing function amplitude (15 N) and period (6 s) for forced vibration (PAGE 50).
limitations_inferred: The approach relies on external precomputed curvature-rigidity curves generated by proprietary software (CableCAD) rather than deriving flexural rigidity from a fully coupled, closed-form contact mechanics formulation within the solver.
Determining the required model parameters requires destructive physical dissection and mechanical push-out testing of cable specimens.
The model requires an artificial least-squares smoothing step after each time increment, indicating potential non-smooth spatial artifacts or numerical instabilities at element boundaries.
External environmental damping (such as aerodynamic drag or fluid interaction) is completely excluded, limiting applicability to isolated cables in non-resistive environments.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The formulated stiffness matrix focuses strictly on bending behavior and does not account for torsion or tension-bending coupling properties (PAGE 47, 57).
Kinetic friction is neglected in the frictional bending formulation (PAGE 14).
The model is restricted by small deformation and small strain assumptions; shear deformation, Poisson's effects, and tension-induced axial elongation are neglected (PAGE 14, 57).
Discontinuous step changes in the EI-curvature curve corresponding to layer slipping events cause abrupt changes in dynamic properties (PAGE 47).

Finite element element length cannot be smaller than the largest half-lay length, imposing a relatively large element size that contributes to numerical error accumulation during time stepping (PAGE 47).
Manufacturing surface imperfections, scratches, and dents on wire surfaces introduced measurement errors and wave-like friction histories during pressure testing (PAGE 47, 66).
Approximating the contact area as the product of outside diameter and specimen length introduces error into the interlayer pressure calculation (PAGE 66).
Differences between experimental and modeled hysteresis loops were influenced by specimen differences and the short 0.3 m cable span being only slightly longer than three lay lengths (PAGE 55).
main_results: The mathematical model demonstrated that cables without external dampers dissipate vibrational energy and experience amplitude decay purely through internal dry friction when bending curvatures are sufficient to induce interlayer wire slip (PAGE 37, 38, 44, 46, 48).

Cable free vibration response clearly separates into a damped phase with decaying amplitude and an undamped phase with sustained small constant amplitude once curvatures fall below the critical slip threshold (PAGE 37, 41, 44, 46).
Predicted end-point displacement histories for a forced cantilever cable agreed with published experimental data from Sauter and Hagedorn within an expected 10% error margin (PAGE 53, 54).
Average interlayer radial pressures determined experimentally from push-out friction tests were 0.475 N/mm^2 between layers 1 and 2, and 0.053 N/mm^2 between layers 2 and 3 (PAGE 63, 65).
The simulated force-displacement hysteresis cycle captured the same slope as experimental observations, although the modeled cycle enclosed a smaller area (PAGE 54, 55).
modeling_methods: One-dimensional continuum formulation for the governing fourth-order nonlinear partial differential equation of motion of transverse cable vibration (PAGE 13, 16, 20).
Variational weak formulation in Sobolev space H1_0(Omega) (PAGE 20, 21).
Finite Element Method (FEM) using fifth-order Hermite interpolation polynomials to ensure continuity of third derivatives of transverse deflection (PAGE 12, 22, 24).
Derivation of elemental consistent mass, stiffness, and stability matrices (PAGE 24, 25).
Newmark direct numerical time integration scheme with linear acceleration (beta = 0.25, gamma = 0.5) for solving dynamic equations (PAGE 12, 26, 27, 28).
Incremental Newton-Raphson iterative formulation for resolving nonlinear equilibrium states (PAGE 29).
Nonlinear flexural rigidity-curvature relationship evaluated via CableCAD software incorporating measured interlayer pressures (PAGE 12, 16, 18).
Post-step least-squares polynomial curve fitting applied to smooth cable displacement configurations across time increments (PAGE 33, 47).
performance_metrics: Vibration displacement amplitude decay over time (PAGE 37, 41, 44, 46, 53).
Sum of squared error between least-squares fitted curve and nodal data points after time iteration (0.0024 reported after first iteration) (PAGE 47, 48).
Percentage error between numerical predictions and experimental displacement measurements (within 10%) (PAGE 53).
Force-displacement hysteresis cycle slope and enclosed hysteresis loop area (PAGE 54, 55).
Maximum theoretical flexural rigidity at zero curvature (EI_max = 64.971 N*m^2 / 6.5 x 10^7 N*mm^2) (PAGE 16, 69).
possible_gap_implications: The phenomenon of curvature-dependent flexural rigidity and energy dissipation driven by interlayer dry friction could potentially inform the mechanical design of friction-based variable-stiffness flexible segments or passive damping elements in compliant mechanical systems, although this thesis focuses exclusively on structural/transmission cables.

The experimental push-out method for quantifying interlayer friction and contact normal pressure could provide a framework for testing multi-layer coiled or braided flexible sheaths and continuum structural elements.

Extending the dynamic formulation to include coupled tension, torsion, and large deformations (as recommended by the author) would be necessary before this modeling approach could be adapted to multi-degree-of-freedom continuum mechanisms or tendons.
paper.research_objective: To develop a mathematical cable model to predict cable vibration and the attendant reduction in vibration amplitude due to internal dry friction caused by relative wire slippage, to create a computer program to analyze cable free vibration using this model, and to verify the validity of the model against published experimental forced vibration data.
paper.research_problem: Long-span cables (such as overhead power transmission lines and cable-stayed structures) suffer from low inherent damping, making them susceptible to vibration damage, while determining their dynamic characteristics is difficult because relative wire slippage between adjacent helical layers causes large, nonlinear variations in flexural rigidity that make analytical solutions impractical.
paper.title: Cable Vibration Considering Internal Friction
